abstract: B-cell leukemia/lymphoma 11B (BCL11B), despite its name, is a key regulator of T-cell development, lineage specification, and T-cell malignancies. BCL11B contains a bipartite DNA-binding domain composed of two C2H2 zinc finger arrays: low-affinity ZF2-3 and high-affinity ZF4-6. These arrays recognize similar six-nucleotide motifs, TG(n)CC(n), as seven of the eight DNA base-contacting residues are conserved between them. The most conserved interactions involve the central GG dinucleotides, recognized by arginine and lysine residues at the key base-interacting positions of ZF3 and ZF5. We determined eight crystal structures of ZF2-3 bound to 12- or 20-base pair DNA duplexes containing either one or two binding motifs. The structures reveal that ZF2-3 recognizes DNA with remarkable configurational flexibility, binding motifs on either the same or opposite DNA strands with variable spacing in three relative orientations: head-to-tail (or tail-to-head), head-to-head, and tail-to-tail. Analysis of BCL11B ChIP-seq peaks revealed a strong enrichment of 1-bp-spaced, same-orientation TGACC(c/t) motif pairs. We also examined six neurodevelopmental disorder-associated missense variants affecting DNA base-contacting residues. Substitutions that replace bulky, positively charged arginine or lysine with smaller or hydrophobic amino acids weaken DNA-binding affinity and specificity, whereas substitutions between asparagine and lysine alter base recognition preferences.
